lead: Six days before Yaldo the readings ask two questions about the Coming One. Where will God dwell? Paul answers: in a people, Jews and Gentiles made one in Christ, built into a temple. Are you really the one? John the Baptist asks from prison, and Jesus answers by pointing to what is happening: the blind see, and the poor hear good news.

set: Paul has reminded the Gentile believers that they were once “far off”, without hope and without God in the world (2:11–13). Now they have been brought near by the blood of Christ. Today's passage explains how. Its background is the deepest social division the first Christians knew: Jew and Gentile, separated by Law, custom and worship.
str: vv. 14–16: Christ is our peace: the wall down, one new humanity, reconciliation through the Cross.
vv. 17–18: peace proclaimed, and access to the Father.
vv. 19–22: the building: citizens, household, temple.
kw: An unusual word. It may recall the barrier in the Jerusalem Temple which kept Gentiles from the inner courts. Josephus describes it, and a stone warning from it, threatening death, was found in 1871. Paul himself was accused of bringing Greeks past it (Acts 21:28).
The right of approach into the presence of a king or to a sanctuary. It occurs again at 3:12.
The foundation stone that sets the line of the whole building (see Isaiah 28:16). The building has one Stone that holds it true.
vv: For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
Peace here is a person, not a treaty. “In his flesh” points to the Cross; it is also the flesh born at Bethlehem.
for through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father.
In one sentence, the whole Trinity and the pattern of all Christian prayer: through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. The great Anaphora of the Holy Qurbono follows this same movement.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
The two words described people without full rights. In God's house there are no second-class members.
in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.
The verb is present and ongoing. The temple is still under construction, and each of us is a living part of it.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this very passage when it speaks of the Jewish people: by his Cross Christ our Peace reconciled Jews and Gentiles, making both one in himself (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism names Christ as the cornerstone of the Church's building (CCC 756).

r.h: Go and tell John what you hear and see
set: V. 1 closes Jesus' instructions to the Twelve (chapter 10). John has been in prison since 4:12. According to Josephus, Herod Antipas held him in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. John had announced one who would come with an axe and fire (3:10–12). What he hears about Jesus sounds rather different.
str: v. 1: Jesus goes on teaching in the towns.
vv. 4–5: Jesus' answer: a list of works that echo Isaiah.
kw: the one who is to come
A title of hope (see Psalm 118:26; Malachi 3:1) and John's own word: “one who is more powerful than I is coming after me” (3:11).
The same verb as John 16:1. To stumble on Jesus means to find him not what we had expected and to turn away.
vv: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?”
The question of this whole season, asked by its greatest preacher.
the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news brought to them.

Jesus does not say yes. He gives a list, woven from Isaiah (35:5–6; 61:1; see also 26:19), and lets John draw his own conclusion. Note where the list ends. After the dead are raised comes what seems small, yet is its climax: good news for the poor.
And blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.”
A beatitude for everyone who has had to give up their own picture of God's way of working.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' signs bear witness that the Father has sent him and invite belief in him, but that they can also be an occasion for “offence” (CCC 548, citing this verse). St John Chrysostom, in his homilies on Matthew, holds that John asked not for himself, but so that his own disciples might go and see (in substance).

qa: The Fathers answered in different ways. Many, with St John Chrysostom, said that John asked for his disciples' sake. Others, and many modern commentators, think the question may be his own: a prisoner who had to wait for Jesus to fulfil God's plan differently than he expected. Either way, Jesus goes on at once to praise him highly (11:7–11). An honest question is not unbelief.
study: Whom do I still treat as a stranger or alien, in my parish, in my town? What would it mean for Christ's peace to break down that wall?
In what way has Jesus not been what I expected? Have I stumbled on it, or learned from it?
